These formations lack a fold test, and their poles cluster (although proximity of poles is expected for the rhyolite and microgranite if, as is believed, they are coeval). The Hobblechain Rhyolite and Packsaddle Microgranite, each with one remanence compo- nent that unblocks at ~ 580°C and another un- blocking at ~ 680°C, have been extensively he- matised and K-metasomatized, as have the underlying Gold Creek Volcanics (Knutson et al., 1979). Therefore, the hematite temperature component is most likely secondary. The ~ 580°C unblocking temperature of the other component suggests that it is carried by magne- tite, presumably a remanent of the original min- eral. This component is therefore interpreted as primary. (A reliable estimate of its direction is obtained only for the Hobblechain Rhyolite, since the directional scatter in the Packsaddle Microgranite is large.) This difference was reflected in thermal demagnetization which gave grouped directions for the lower half, but highly scattered directions above (Fig. 7a). Since the upper sequence crops out on hill tops, light- ning strikes seem a possible cause of the scatter. Therefore, the seven remaining specimens were demagnetised partly by AF before thermal treat- ment. This procedure removed a low-coercivity component (cf. Figs. 7c and 7d) and greatly re- duced the scatter, leaving only one discordant direction (Fig. 7b). Two positively inclined remanence compo- nents, I and H, were resolved in each "lower" sample; component I unblocked at ~ 580 ° C, and component H at ~ 680 °C (Figs. 7e and 7f ). Only H was resolved in the "upper" samples. The or- thogonal plots of three samples contained evi- dence of a third component in the form of short linear segments between 580°C and 650°C (Comp. 3 in Fig. 7f). This component was not resolved, but it appears to have a northerly, neg- ative inclination. The combined bedding-corrected direct

ples had well-defined direc- tions, giving a component H that unblocked at ~680°C. In seventeen of the samples H had shallow inclinations to the northwest; in the eighteenth, H was inclined to the southeast (Fig. 9d). The bedding-corrected mean, after inver- sion of the SE direction, is 288.2 °, -5.3 ° (Ot95___8.1 o ). This is similar to the mean direc- tions of the upper Tawallah Group (Table 2). Settlement Creek Volcanics Ten dark-grey mafic samples were collected from the upper part of the Volcanics (Locality 2 ). Bedding was not evident at the site, and the site tilt correction was estimated from nearby in- terbedded sediments and the Wollogorang For- mation. Because of large variations in bedding dips, this estimate is approximate. Most specimens were demagnetized by AF, others thermally, revealing two components, I (intermediate) and H (high), distinguished by differences in coercivity and unblocking temper- atures. The I component, which dominated the remanence, was removed at 15-100 mT or just below 600°C. It yielded a scattered group of WNW directions with negative inclinations (Fig. 4c) and a bedding-corrected mean 291.1 °, -25.6 ° (o~95= 16 ° ). Jackson et al. (1987) note that the Settlement Creek Volcanics are hydro- thermally altered. This was confirmed in thin sections cut from palaeomagnetic samples. Therefore, component I is probably secondary. Because of scatter, the direction of H could be defined in only 11 out of the 26 samples, and sometimes only by anchor- ing the principal component linear segment to the origin. However, in most samples its polarity was evident in the orthogonal projection plots. The remanence directions before and after bedding corrections are shown in Figs. 5c and 5d). Bedding correction increased the direc- tional scatter of the I component, for which the fold test of McFadden (1990) was negative at the 99% confidence level (Table 3 ). Thus I is an overprint. Mc- Fadden's fold test for H was inconclusive, but McElhinny's (1964) test showed the reduction to be statistically significant at 95% confidence level (Table 3 ), suggesting that H was acquired before deformation. of the Tawallah Group: the Settlement Creek Volcanics, Hobblechain Rhyolite and Packsaddle Microgranite. These formations lack a fold test, and their poles cluster (although proximity of poles is expected for the rhyolite and microgranite if, as is believed, they are coeval). The Hobblechain Rhyolite and Packsaddle Microgranite, each with one remanence compo- nent that unblocks at ~ 580°C and another un- blocking at ~ 680°C, have been extensively he- matised and K-metasomatized, as have the underlying Gold Creek Volcanics (Knutson et al., 1979). Therefore, the hematite temperature component is most likely secondary. The ~ 580°C unblocking temperature of the other component suggests that it is carried by magne- tite, presumably a remanent of the original min- eral. This component is therefore interpreted as primary. (A reliable estimate of its direction is obtained only for the Hobblechain Rhyolite, since the directional scatter in the Packsaddle Microgranite is large.) It should be noted that thin section, XRD and Raman Spectroscopy studies of two typical samples did not reveal magnetite (they showed hematite and, possibly, maghemite); however, remanent magnetite may occur as inclusions and may therefore be too small to be resolved by those methods. Knutson et al. (1979) attributed the regional metasomatism at Localities 4-6 to hydrothermal fluids related to the formation of numerous brec- cia pipes. (The fluid temperature of associated carbonate deposition was estimated as 150- 300 ° C, well below the unblocking temperature of the magnetite component. ) The minimum age of the pipes is not clear from field relationships. However, Knutson et al. suggested that they formed soon after the extrusion of the volcanics, e.g., as late-stage hydrothermal products of the same magmatic cycle, whereas Wall and Hein- rich (1990) suggest that the pipes were pro- duced later during regional tectonism. While the results do not indicate the age of the pipes, the directional similarity of the magnetite and he- matite components does favour the suggestion that the regional K-metasomatism occurred soon after the units were emplaced (Knutson et al., 1979). These formations lack a fold test, and their poles cluster (although proximity of poles is expected for the rhyolite and microgranite if, as is believed, they are coeval). The Hobblechain Rhyolite and Packsaddle Microgranite, each with one remanence compo- nent that unblocks at ~ 580°C and another un- blocking at ~ 680°C, have been extensively he- matised and K-metasomatized, as have the underlying Gold Creek Volcanics (Knutson et al., 1979). Therefore, the hematite temperature component is most likely secondary. The ~ 580°C unblocking temperature of the other component suggests that it is carried by magne- tite, presumably a remanent of the original min- eral. This component is therefore interpreted as primary. (A reliable estimate of its direction is obtained only for the Hobblechain Rhyolite, since the directional scatter in the Packsaddle Microgranite is large.) Sampling procedures and measurements About 1800 samples were collected. The em- phasis was on the upper Tawallah, McArthur, and Nathan Groups, because of their generally good exposures and stratigraphic continuities. Fig. l shows the sampling localities. Most are in the Batten Trough where the McArthur and Nathan Groups have their maximum known thicknesses and where streams have incised an uplifted ter- rain to expose the strata. The majority of sam- ples was collected along two traverses. The first, a composite of several stratigraphic sections along the Kilgour River and its tributaries, spans a 900 m thickness of the upper Tawallah to mid- dle McArthur Groups. The average stratigraphic interval for sampling was 1 m. The second trav- erse, on the northwestern flanks of the Abner Range, spans a 900 m thickness of the Nathan Group and was sampled at an average interval of 2.5 m. The reman- ences were measured principally on a 2-axis ScT cryogenic magnetometer, with specimen inver- sion to obtain eight readings for each measure- ment. Demagnetization was by standard alter- nating field (AF) and thermal techniques: the former using either a Schonstedt 2-axis GSD-5 demagnetizer or a 2-axis instrument described by Senanayake (1981); the latter in a Schonstedt TSD- 1 demagnetizer or in large-volume furnaces described by McElhinny et al. Introduction The Precambrian APWP for Australia has been determined mainly from remanence directions of dated igneous units. Such directions, while es- sential for age calibration, are likely to leave large gaps because of the intermittent and sporadic nature of igneous activity. Sedimentary se- quences generally provide more continuous geo- logic re

Besides their use in polar wander studies, sed- imentary sequences may also provide a record of geomagnetic reversals with applications to cor- relation and dating of rock units. So far, only very few attempts to set up a reversal stratigraphy for correlation have been reported for the Precam- brian (Evans et al., 1975; Bingham and Evans, 1976; Elston and Bressler, 1980; Elston, 1984; Thomas and Piper, 1992 ). This is partly because of the difficulty of separating and identifying primary remanences in partially overprinted rocks and partly because of the lack of suitable continuous sequences. In Australia work has been limited to a narrow interval spanning the Pre- cambrian-Cambrian boundary (Kirschvink, 1978; Burek et al., 1979; Chamalaun et al., 1989 ). This paper describes a polar wander and po- larity reversal study of a part of the Palaeo-Me- soproterozoic McArthur Basin of northern Aus- tralia (Fig. 1 ). Introduction The Precambrian APWP for Australia has been determined mainly from remanence directions of dated igneous units. Such directions, while es- sential for age calibration, are likely to leave large gaps because of the intermittent and sporadic nature of igneous activity. Sedimentary se- quences generally provide more continuous geo- logic re

in the Pre- cambrian where path segments may have to be fitted to a few, widely spaced poles, leaving the direction of polar wander doubtful. Besides their use in polar wander studies, sed- imentary sequences may also provide a record of geomagnetic reversals with applications to cor- relation and dating of rock units. So far, only very few attempts to set up a reversal stratigraphy for correlation have been reported for the Precam- brian (Evans et al., 1975; Bingham and Evans, 1976; Elston and Bressler, 1980; Elston, 1984; Thomas and Piper, 1992 ). This is partly because of the difficulty of separating and identifying primary remanences in partially overprinted rocks and partly because of the lack of suitable continuous sequences. In Australia work has been limited to a narrow interval spanning the Pre- cambrian-Cambrian boundary (Kirschvink, 1978; Burek et al., 1979; Chamalaun et al., 1989 ). This paper describes a polar wander and po- larity reversal study of a part of the Palaeo-Me- soproterozoic McArthur Basin of northern Aus- tralia (Fig. 1 ). The basin comprises sediments, and minor volcanics and intrusives, which to- gether form the platform cover on a Palaeopro- terozoic basement. The sequences appear to be unmetamorphosed, but have in some regions be

s up to at least 12 kin. The present study concerns its southeastern part (Figs. 1 and 2) which contains both clastics and carbonates. Most rocks of this region were formed during a ~ 100 m.y. period centred around 1670 Ma for which the Austra- lian APWP has few dated poles. At some locali- ties the outcrop is sufficiently continuous and extensive for polarity reversal studies. Preliminary results of this work, based on rel- atively few samples, have been described earlier (Plumb, 1985; Idnurm and Giddings, 1988 ). A1- though the preliminary pole positions are re- vised, the pole trajectory needs little change. However, several remanences that were tenta- tively assumed to be primary now turn out to be overprints, leading to considerable modifica- tions in the polarity pattern. A related study of thick sequences of predominantly quartz sand- stones and conglomerates of the Kombolgie For- mation in the northwestern McArthur Basin will be reported separately. 1. I. Introduction The Precambrian APWP for Australia has been determined mainly from remanence directions of dated igneous units. Such directions, while es- sential for age calibration, are likely to leave large gaps because of the intermittent and sporadic nature of igneous activity. Sedimentary se- quences generally provide more continuous geo- logic re

in the Pre- cambrian where path segments may have to be fitted to a few, widely spaced poles, leaving the direction of polar wander doubtful. Besides their use in polar wander studies, sed- imentary sequences may also provide a record of geomagnetic reversals with applications to cor- relation and dating of rock units. So far, only very few attempts to set up a reversal stratigraphy for correlation have been reported for the Precam- brian (Evans et al., 1975; Bingham and Evans, 1976; Elston and Bressler, 1980; Elston, 1984; Thomas and Piper, 1992 ). This is partly because of the difficulty of separating and identifying primary remanences in partially overprinted rocks and partly because of the lack of suitable continuous sequences. In Australia work has been limited to a narrow interval spanning the Pre- cambrian-Cambrian boundary (Kirschvink, 1978; Burek et al., 1979; Chamalaun et al., 1989 ). This paper describes a polar wander and po- larity reversal study of a part of the Palaeo-Me- soproterozoic McArthur Basin of northern Aus- tralia (Fig. 1 ). The basin comprises sediments, and minor volcanics and intrusives, which to- gether form the platform cover on a Palaeopro- terozoic basement. The sequences appear to be unmetamorphosed, but have in some regions be

s up to at least 12 kin. The present study concerns its southeastern part (Figs. 1 and 2) which contains both clastics and carbonates. Most rocks of this region were formed during a ~ 100 m.y. period centred around 1670 Ma for which the Austra- lian APWP has few dated poles. At some locali- ties the outcrop is sufficiently continuous and extensive for polarity reversal studies. Preliminary results of this work, based on rel- atively few samples, have been described earlier (Plumb, 1985; Idnurm and Giddings, 1988 ). A1- though the preliminary pole positions are re- vised, the pole trajectory needs little change. However, several remanences that were tenta- tively assumed to be primary now turn out to be overprints, leading to considerable modifica- tions in the polarity pattern. A related study of thick sequences of predominantly quartz sand- stones and conglomerates of the Kombolgie For- mation in the northwestern McArthur Basin will be reported separately. 1. I. Sampling procedures and measurements About 1800 samples were collected. The em- phasis was on the upper Tawallah, McArthur, and Nathan Groups, because of their generally good exposures and stratigraphic continuities. Fig. l shows the sampling localities. Most are in the Batten Trough where the McArthur and Nathan Groups have their maximum known thicknesses and where streams have incised an uplifted ter- rain to expose the strata. The majority of sam- ples was collected along two traverses. The first, a composite of several stratigraphic sections along the Kilgour River and its tributaries, spans a 900 m thickness of the upper Tawallah to mid- dle McArthur Groups. The average stratigraphic interval for sampling was 1 m. The second trav- erse, on the northwestern flanks of the Abner Range, spans a 900 m thickness of the Nathan Group and was sampled at an average interval of 2.5 m. Several units were sampled elsewhere in the fault zone or near the eastern margin of the basin. The traverses are shown i

inants from drilling. Approximately 2000 specimens were demag- netised stepwise at the Black Mountain Palaeo- magnetic Laboratory in Canberra. The reman- ences were measured principally on a 2-axis ScT cryogenic magnetometer, with specimen inver- sion to obtain eight readings for each measure- ment. Demagnetization was by standard alter- nating field (AF) and thermal techniques: the former using either a Schonstedt 2-axis GSD-5 demagnetizer or a 2-axis instrument described by Senanayake (1981); the latter in a Schonstedt TSD- 1 demagnetizer or in large-volume furnaces described by McElhinny et al. (1971). In pre- liminary work, thermal demagnetization gave usually less scattered orthogonal projection plots than AF demagnetization, and was therefore adopted for most subsequent measurements. However, for several sites thermal demagnetiza- tion alone gave large, directional scatters be- tween samples. For these sites, samples were par- tially demagnetized by AF at peak intensities up to 100 mT before thermal treatment--a proce- dure that has successfully removed lightning-in- duced overprints (Cox, 1961; Graham, 1961; Purucker, 1974). Magnetic susceptibilities were monitored between heatings using a Collinson and Molyneux (1967) type instrument. Remanence components were determ

ly at a mean angular deviation (MAD) of < 5 °; if this number was less than 20 the angle was < 7 °. The formation mean directions were calculated from sample averages if more than one remanence di- rection was available; otherwise the specimen di- rection was used. Directions deviating by more than 60 ° from the mean were excluded from the final analysis. Polarity assignment for some parts of the re- versal column was complicated by the destruc- tion of primary remanence by magnetic over- printing. However, even though the remanence directions could not be determined, the polarity was sometimes discernible. The reversal dia- grams show the inclination and declination of the primary directions, if available. Polarity-only data are indicated by square symbols. 3. T. 260 I, Australia Received 6 April 1994; revised version accepted 20 July 1994 Abstract Approximately 1800 samples from volcanic, clastic and carbonate sequences of the southeastern McArthur Basin in northern Australia were analysed palaeomagnetically to define in detail the Australian apparent polar wander path (APWP) for a period centred at ~ 1670 Ma and to develop a Proterozoic reversal stratigraphy for correlation and dating. Twelve palaeomagnetic poles are interpreted as primary,, including two that are preliminary. These increase the Australian palaeomagnetic database for the Proterozoic by ~ 30%. Another ten poles record three, or possibly four, periods of overprinting. The study also yields one of the oldest reversal records reported so far

However, mottling and other weath- ering indicators are absent at the sites (most Wollogorang Formation samples containing the overprint have no hematite pigment; most Ame- lia Dolomite samples, although red, are silici- fled), and the overprint has only one polarity, unlike remanences produced by Tertiary weath- ering (e.g., Idnurm and Senior, 1978). The OP2 group marks the apex of a hairpin bend in the path. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: S Standard palaeomagnetic specimens (24 mm high) were prepared from the oriented core samples, and their remanent magnetization was measured with a Schonstedt DSM-1 Spinner magnetometer. Specimens were demag- netized by stepwise alternating-field (AF) and thermal methods, using a Schonstedt GSD-1 AF demagnetizer and a Schonstedt TSD-1 furnace, and results for each specimen were plotted on orthogonal vector diagrams (Zijderveld 1967) as well as on equal-area projections. Demagnetization trajectories were interpreted by fitting straight lines through the data points. Great circles were used for a few samples (site NT) when planar demagnetization trajectories were identified. The magnetic carriers in these volcanic rocks were investigated using a number of different rock magnetic techniques, as well as microscopic observations. Isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) acquisition experiments were performed on unheated core specimens at room temperature (20°C), in applied fields of up to 1.2 tesla (T). This IRM was demagnetized by a stepwise thermal method. Thermomagnetic experiments were also conducted with an automated Brucker Curie balance. GEOLOGICAL CONTEXT The volcanics of Sidi-Said-Maschou, located about 50 km east of El Jadida (Fig. l), were first described by Gigout (1956). These rocks crop out in the valley of Oum-er-Rbia River, north of Sidi-Said-Makhou (especially at the base of Sidi-Moul-Nker) and in some tributary valleys (particularly near K. Sbal). The volcanic rocks are included in a shaly-silty succession with green shales overlain by purple shales with trilobite-bearing pink limestones levels. Purple shales and siltstones are in close relation with lava flows and sills: they appear with the first lava flows and their last occurrence slightly precedes the end of the volcanic activity. The whole succession is cut by vertical dykes. Gigout (1956) described a section with dykes, sills and lava flows at the base of Sidi-Moul-Nker. In contrast correlative dolerites from nunataks in north Greenland of the same polarity as the bulk of the south Greenland dykes yield a pole position (231 "E, 10.3 ON, Abrahamsen & Van der Voo 1987) close to the A2 pole. Orientation of the samples was by magnetic compass, but the values do not appear to have been affected by the magnetism of the rocks, despite the variable NRM intensity. Palaeomagnetic directions for the lower and upper lavas are statistically distinguished: the difference in palaeomag- netic directions between the data sets of these lava flows is 13.3", with an uncertainty (95 per cent confidence) of 3.7". lava flows were sampled in the Puru area (36"15'N; 81'30'E) north of the Altyn Tagh fault. The sampling sites were distributed between 13 km and 18km from the fault. The two lavas are dated by K-Ar methods to be 1.05 f 0.11 and 1.44 f 0.06 Ma. Their palaeomagnetic directions show reversed polarity of the Matuyama chron. Declination values for nine sampling sites on the upper lava flow more than 14 km from the fault are concordant, with little variance (D = -166.3", I = -50.8", = 2.2"), but declination at a site nearer the fault (13 km from it) (D = -173.7") displays a counter-clockwise deflection of 7.4" f 5.2" from that of the other sites. This palaeomagnetic rotation is ascribed to tectonic rotation due to left-lateral slip on the Altyn Tagh fault during the last 1.0myr. The area beyond 13 km from the fault, however, does not provide any evidence for the large rotation (-60") expected from the known strike-slip movement of 30 mm yr-'. This implies that little deformation penetrates deep into the Tarim craton from the fault. The lack of deformation of features along the Altyn Tagh fault is explained by the non-rigid behaviour of the narrow zone of the continental lithosphere near the fault and/or by low stress acting on the fault. Key words: Altyn Tagh fault, K-Ar da

tyn Tagh, Karakorum, Kunlun and Red River Faults (Molnar & Tapponnier 1975; Tapponnier et al. 1982) (Fig. 1). We focused on the Altyn Tagh fault in the Tibetan Plateau to detect crustal rotation, because it is one of the world's greatest strike-slip faults (Molnar & Tapponnier 1975; Peltzer, Tapponnier & Armijo 1989). The Altyn Tagh fault follows the northern margin of the Tibetan highlands for nearly 2000 km. The rate of the Holocene left-lateral slip of the Altyn Tagh has been estimated to be 30 i 20 mm per year from the Quaternary offsets of moraines and erosional features (Peltzer, Tapponnier & Armijo 1989). We have collected samples from Pleistocene basaltic andesite lava flows near Puru village (36'08"; 81'26'E) (Fig. 1). We have measured the palaeomagnetism and K-Ar ages of these lavas in an attempt to examine the rotation properties associated with deformation along the fault. GEOLOGICAL SETTING AND SAMPLING The Puru area lies on the southern margin of the Tarim Craton, which is bounded to the south by the Songban- Ganzi Terrane (Dewey er al. 1988). The Kunlun-Qinling Suture marks the boundary between the two terranes. It marks the southern limit of the composite Eurasian plate before the accretion of the Songban-Ganzi Terrane in the late Triassic. The A

The Natural Remanent Magnetization (NRM) was measured using a JR-4 spinner magnetometer (Geofyzika, Brno). Thermal demagnetization was performed using a cylindrical furnace, with a fast heating rate, and cooling by forced air at the heating site. Selected thermal increments were 100" to 200 "C treatment, and 50-20 "C for higher temperatures. Reduced temperature increments were used at the highest temperatures in order to obtain a precise determination of the magnetization evolution. Alternating field treatments up to 160mT were attempted using an apparatus which automatically cancels the parasitic anhysteretic effect (Le Goff 1985), but blocking field values in these specimens were too high to permit any significant demagnetization by this means. Ante-tilting magnetization The positive inversion test, for samples with normal ChRM and a reversed second component, shows that the two components were in this case acquired in a relatively short time interval, and the assumption of overprinting or diagenesis during two polarity intervals remains possible in this case. The fact, that the high blocking temperature component is always of normal polarity is consistent with the hypothesis of a primary magnetization, because of the large dominance of the normal polarity during the Late Triassic-Lower Lias period (Hailwood 1989). Similarly, the presence of a weak second anti-parallel component, in some beds, is not surprising if the assumption of diagenesis of long duration is taken into account. Older formations of the same basin underwent only Permian and recent overprints (Henry et al. 1991, 1992c) and the single event which specifically affected the Zarzaitine levels is a rubefaction. It confirms, from Autunian to Lias, a latitudinal displacement of stable Africa towards the north, with important anti-clockwise rotation contrary to Laurussia which did not undergo significant rotation. This transition of Pangea from A2 to A ended before the Late Triassic. he collection was studied in the palaeomagnetic laboratory of the Institute of Geology, Rennes University, France. Two cubic specimens from a hand sample were heated in up to 15 steps using a Schonstedt TSD-1 demagnetizer. Measure- ments were made on a LET1 cryogenic magnetometer with the noise level at about 1 X lO-'Am-'. Components isolated from two specimens from a sample were used for calculations of sample means, which in turn were used for computation of the formation mean. Anisotropy was measured on one or two specimens from a sample with a Digico magnetometer. Other studies included chemical analyses, optic observations on thin sections, scanning electron microscopy and rock-magnetic experiments. Chemical analyses revealed that the main portion of iron resides in a phase that dissolves in concentrated hydrochloride acid, whereas the part of iron dissolved in weak acid is several-fold less; the share of iron in siderite and silicates is negligible. he collection was studied in the palaeomagnetic laboratory of the Institute of Geology, Rennes University, France. Two cubic specimens from a hand sample were heated in up to 15 steps using a Schonstedt TSD-1 demagnetizer. Measure- ments were made on a LET1 cryogenic magnetometer with the noise level at about 1 X lO-'Am-'. Components isolated from two specimens from a sample were used for calculations of sample means, which in turn were used for computation of the formation mean. Anisotropy was measured on one or two specimens from a sample with a Digico magnetometer. Other studies included chemical analyses, optic observations on thin sections, scanning electron microscopy and rock-magnetic experiments. RESULTS The NRM intensities of the red beds range from 2 to 10, about 4 X lo-' A m-' on average. A sample of brick-red coarse-grained porous sandstone completely remagnetized by the present-day field is rejected. After removal of a weak dispersed remanence at 200" to 250 "C, practically noiseless orthogonal plots are obtained for 21 remaining samples. Maximal K,,, and intermediate K,,, axes of anisotropy ellipsoids gravitate to the stereonet equator (Fig. 4). Some preferences in K,,, and K,,, orientation are noticeable, but, taking into account the almost perfect equality of the two parameters, this is hardly significant. Unfortunately, a more distinct correlation is not found between palaeomagnetic properties, e.g. the length of the great circle segment, and K,,, orientation or degree of anisotropy. Rock-magnetic studies revealed high uniformity of the collection. All isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) curves are very similar (Fig. Sa), and no correlation between directions of the NRM and IRM behaviour was found. Thermal demagnetization of the saturation magnetization also reveals rather uniform magnetic properties (Fig. 5b). In the latter figure, weak irregularities are noticeable on curves for samples tu6 and tu20, but they are not correlated with palaeomagnetic data: samples tu6 and tu7 have the strongest anisotropy and well-defined remagnetization circles, whereas samples tul and tu20 have very weak anisotropy and no shift of vector endpoints on stereonet. mples tu6 and tu7 have the strongest anisotropy and well-defined remagnetization circles, whereas samples tul and tu20 have very weak anisotropy and no shift of vector endpoints on stereonet. Chemical analyses revealed that the main portion of iron resides in a phase that dissolves in concentrated hydrochloride acid, whereas the part of iron dissolved in weak acid is several-fold less; the share of iron in siderite and silicates is negligible. Thus, these analyses together with rock-magnetic and palaeomagnetic data point to haematite as the main iron compound and the only NRM carrier in these rocks. Detrital grains often distinctly concentrate to boundaries between thin layers; the cross-bedded parts with high concentration of opaque minerals often display a one-sided feather-like pattern. Each independent bed was considered as a sampling site. Generally, five oriented cores (2.54 cm diameter) were obtained from each site. Sampling was carried out with a portable drill and samples were oriented with both magnetic and sun compasses, where possible. A total of 83 cores, from 19 sites, were collected. 22. PALAEOMAGNETIC STUDY The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) and bulk susceptibility of till specimens were initially measured. In order to determine the different magnetic components that integrate to form the NRM and to analyse their magnetic stability, pilot samples were submitted to stepwise AF demagnetization, thermal demagnetization or chemical leaching. Two sedimentary cycles developed in the Late Palaeozoic and Cretaceous Tertiary, the latter interrupted by the Andean Orogeny in the Late Tertiary. This produced most of the structural features of the region. From a structural point of view the Sierras Subandinas are made up of a series of asymmetric anticlines, generally trending N to NE with vergence to the east. The sequence exposed at the sampling localities starts with Arenigian to Llanvirnian clastic sediments (Monaldi, Boso & Fernandez 1986), separated by an erosional unconformity from the diamictites of the Zapla Formation (Schlagintweit 1943). The origin of this unit is controversial, as some authors have assigned to it a glaciomarine origin (Schlagintweit 1943; Turner 1960), while others attribute it to a sudden subsidence of the basin (Cuerda & Antelo 1973; Antelo 1978). This is conformably overlain by the claystones and sandstones of the Lipeon Formation (Turner 1960), which contains some ferriferous horizons near its basis. Thirteen dolerite dykes, out of a swarm of more than 200, all belonging to the supposed Precambrian N-S to NE-SW striking dyke swarm on Bornholm, have been sampled and palaeomagnetically investigated. The dykes vary in thickness between 0.2 and 60m and are intruded in Precambrian gneisses and granites of Gothian and/or Subjotnian (1 650-1280 Ma) age. Principal component analysis of detailed AF and some thermal demagnetization experiments reveal three groups of stable direction clusterings from the dykes investigated. The stable remanent magnetization of the major dyke Keldse2 dyke and the baked gneiss contact corresponds to a palaeomagnetic mean pole (group A). The result is confirmed by dual polarities and a positive baked contact test. A recent series of overviews and guides of the geology of Bornholm was published by Surlyk (1980) and Berthelsen (1980,1989,1992a,b, 1993). About three-quarters of the Pre-Quaternary surface of Bornholm consists of Precambrian (Proterozoic) gneisses and granite (Noe-Nygaard 1963), while the rest is covered by Palaeozoic and Mesozoic sediments. The bedrock is poorly exposed because of glacial drift, but along the north-east coast exposures are excellent. In this study, samples have been collected from the youngest members of the Komarov Volcanic Complex, the Kralov Dvur Formation, the overlying Hirnantian diamictite horizons and from the Kosov Formation (Table 1 and Fig. 1 ). A baked contact test was conducted on these sedimentary (three sites) and igneous (four sites) rocks. The attitude of the volcanic horizons was determined from immediately overlying sediments. section_candidates.excerpt: 93 March 9 SUMMARY Extensive geological, geophysical and geochronological data available from the Canary Islands establish conclusively that formation of the oldest subaerial volcanic structure of the islands began during the Miocene. A mid-Cretaceous age for these volcanic formations has been postulated in previous works on the basis of palaeomagnetic determinatiods. The results obtained in the present palaeomagnetic study of Lanzarote include analysis of the record of variations of magnetic inclination in boreholes that penetrate the whole of the oldest volcanic series. They show that the excessive age previously assigned to these formations is due to the utilization of volcanic units with abnormally low (<lSo) magnetic inclinations (LGIs). section_candidates.excerpt: 93 March 9 SUMMARY Extensive geological, geophysical and geochronological data available from the Canary Islands establish conclusively that formation of the oldest subaerial volcanic structure of the islands began during the Miocene. A mid-Cretaceous age for these volcanic formations has been postulated in previous works on the basis of palaeomagnetic determinatiods. The results obtained in the present palaeomagnetic study of Lanzarote include analysis of the record of variations of magnetic inclination in boreholes that penetrate the whole of the oldest volcanic series. They show that the excessive age previously assigned to these formations is due to the utilization of volcanic units with abnormally low (<lSo) magnetic inclinations (LGIs). The units stratigraphically beneath and above the LGI horizons give, in fact, directions consistent with the Middle-Upper Miocene field direction (D = 359", I = 45", with k = 29, a95 = 6.7" and a palaeopole of 87"N, 178"E), thereby confirming the Miocene age of the oldest subaerial volcanics of Lanzarote. Short excursions of the geomagnetic field seem likely to be the explanation for these LGIs, since other factors such as tectonic tilting, post-eruptive modification of the primary remanence or errors in sample orientation can be disregarded. Recent investigations have shown, however, that volcanic rocks can record anomalously the direction of the geomagnetic field, giving data that can bring about erroneous interpretations in the dating of the volcanic formations in which they are observed. Received 1995 January 13; in original form 1994 June 30 SUMMARY An Early Proterozoic palaeomagnetic signature (c. 2125 Ma), verified by a positive conglomerate test, is recorded in the Kuetsyarvi Formation, Pechenga Group (north-west Russia), but the majority of the palaeomagnetic directions observed in the Pechenga Group lithologies reflect a low-grade remagnetization event probably linked with the Late Precambrian Baikalian Orogeny which affected north-west Russia and northern Norway. Secondary pyrrhotite is. the dominant remanence carrier in the uppermost formations of the Pechenga Group. Palaeomagnetic poles from the Kuetsyarvi Formation differ somewhat or partially overlap with coeval palaeomagnetic poles from other tectonomagmatic provinces in northern Fennoscandia, but it is premature at this stage to speculate on intraplate movements during the Early Proterozoic. Besides, the Kuetsyarvi Formation probably developed during an early phase of intracontinental rifting along the northern margin of Fennoscandia, similar to the present-day East African rift. The iron sulphides are principally pyrite and pyrrhotite where the pyrrhotite is a secondary low-grade metamorphic phase replacing pyrite (Abzalov, Both & Brewer 1993). palaeomagnetic directions observed in the Pechenga Group lithologies reflect a low-grade remagnetization event probably linked with the Late Precambrian Baikalian Orogeny which affected north-west Russia and northern Norway. Secondary pyrrhotite is. the dominant remanence carrier in the uppermost formations of the Pechenga Group. Palaeomagnetic poles from the Kuetsyarvi Formation differ somewhat or partially overlap with coeval palaeomagnetic poles from other tectonomagmatic provinces in northern Fennoscandia, but it is premature at this stage to speculate on intraplate movements during the Early Proterozoic. Besides, the Kuetsyarvi Formation probably developed during an early phase of intracontinental rifting along the northern margin of Fennoscandia, similar to the present-day East African rift. Palaeolatitude estimates from the Kuetsyarvi Formation suggest that the Pechenga region was located in latitudes of around 20" to 30" during the 2100-2200Ma interval. The radiometric age (U-Pb) of the rocks, stated as 420 T 20 Ma, places them in the Silurian. A palaeomagnetic study reveals the presence of four groups of palaeomagnetic poles. One of these is derived from an isolated component representing Permian overprinting. According to this interpretation, the ophiolitic complex would not have been involved in tectonic action after Silurian times. On the other hand, this component does not agree with the results of the neighbouring Bohemian Massif but is consistent with Late Carboniferous data of the European Variscans. In this case the other two components should be interpreted as Early- to Mid-Carboniferous overprints. This interpretation implies important strike-slip movements. GEOLOGIAL SETTING The Sudetes form the north-eastern extremity of the Bohemian Massif, which lies in the eastern part of the European Variscan Belt (Fig. 1). They consist of a variety of small domains exhibiting different lithostratigraphic, tectonic and metamorphic characteristics. The massif itself is cut by the Marginal Sudetic Fault (MSF) striking NW-SE. Received 1995 March 7; in original form 1993 December 10 SUMMARY The investigated material comprises rocks of the Palaeozoic ophiolitic assemblage exposed around the Sowie G6ry Mountains Massif in the Sudetes in the form of the three units: Slqia, Zqbkowice and Nowa Ruda. The radiometric age (U-Pb) of the rocks, stated as 420 T 20 Ma, places them in the Silurian. A palaeomagnetic study reveals the presence of four groups of palaeomagnetic poles. One of these is derived from an isolated component representing Permian overprinting. The second remanence component fits with the Silurian results from Baltica and may therefore be regarded as being of Silurian age. According to this interpretation, the ophiolitic complex would not have been involved in tectonic action after Silurian times. On the other hand, this component does not agree with the results of the neighbouring Bohemian Massif but is consistent with Late Carboniferous data of the European Variscans. In this case the other two components should be interpreted as Early- to Mid-Carboniferous overprints. This interpretation implies important strike-slip movements. In order to exclude one of these hypotheses, more data are still

span are the most scarce and uncertain. For this reason, the authors decided to undertake a palaeomagnetic study of rocks of the Silurian ophiolitic assemblages from the Sudetes. GEOLOGIAL SETTING The Sudetes form the north-eastern extremity of the Bohemian Massif, which lies in the eastern part of the European Variscan Belt (Fig. 1). They consist of a variety of small domains exhibiting different lithostratigraphic, tectonic and metamorphic characteristics. Low-grade metamorphosed or even unmetamorphosed mafic to ultramafic complexes, which can be considered as remnants of oceanic crust, surround the Precambrian allochthonous gneissic massif of the Sowie G6ry Mountains (Fig. 1). The massif itself is cut by the Marginal Sudetic Fault (MSF) striking NW-SE. Recent radiometric dating assigns a Late Carboniferous-Early Permian age (298 Ma) to the previously 'Middle Permian' rhyolitic volcanism of the northern Vosges. A palaeomagnetic study was undertaken on rhyolites of the Nideck-Donon massif and on neighbouring Permian basins (VillC, Saint-Die) in order to obtain a new pole for the Early Permian and to detect overprints. The NRM of rhyolites and tuffs can be described by almost univectorial magnetizations (Fig. 2). Unblocking temperatures are generally high (650-680 "C). In some sites (Ni3, 9, 10, 14, 15, 33, Vi3, FN6), components with intermediate temperatures of 580-600 "C represent at least 90 per cent of the NRM. The residual has unblocking temperatures of 650-680 "C. In other sites (Ni 5, 21, 22, 24, 29, 30, FN 5), both intermediate- and high-temperature components coexist with comparable intensities. Isothermal remanent magnetization curves (IRM) and thermal demag- netization of a three-component IRM generally indicate the presence of both low-coercivity, intermediate-temperature (580 "C) minerals and high-coercivity, high-unblocking- temperature (660-680 "C) minerals in variable proportions (Fig. 3). In the microgranite Ni33 the low-coercivity, intermediate-temperature minerals account for the major part of the induced magnetization (Ni33.52, Fig. 3). The same behaviour is observed for the NRM (Ni 33.52, Fig. 2). The carrier of the intermediate-temperature remanence is interpreted as being magnetite, while the high-temperature residual is carried by haematite. Vosges are arkosic sandstones characterized by well-sorted, rounded grains with tangential high-angle cross bedding. These characteristics are typical of dune facies emplaced in an aeolian environment (Hollinger 1978). Three sites were sampled but did not provide results that could be interpreted Alteration of the magmatic rocks In magmatic rocks, clay minerals, sericite or minor calcite often replace feldspars. Mafic minerals such as amphiboles are completely altered. However, biotites remain well preserved, hence it is possible to date them by radiometric processing (Montigny, in Schneider et al. 1994). Oxides consist mainly of haematite and titano-haemitite associated with rutile, but relics of titano-magnetite and ilmenite are also present. The glassy groundmasses of the effusive and pyroclastic rocks are completely devitrified. Felsitic and spherolitic textures are common. Volcanic glass of the groundmass, pumice and glass shards are replaced by cryptocrystalline aggregates of silica and alkali feldspars or by chlorite and calcite. All these observations strongly indicate that the volcanics underwent hydrothermal alteration during and after cooling. A logarithmic plot of hysteresis parameters (Figure 5h) shows that rocks with unblocking temperatures below 600øC have consistently higher Hcr/Hc ratios and lower Mrs/Ms ratios, suggesting that contributions from multidomain (MD) grains are important. MD grains may carry the magnetizations we interpret as recent viscous overprints. Reflected light microscopy indicates a marked contrast in ox- ide mineralogy and textures between the nonhematitic and red (hematitic) rocks in both sections. In nonhematitic sandstones, visible iron oxides (mostly specular-hematite and magnetite) ap- pear as angular to slightly embayed and fractured detrital grains (a few to tens of microns in size). Magnetite grains lack exsolu- tion textures and hematite grains are homogeneous. Fine-grained hematite pigment in white sandstones is rare. Detrital iron oxides in rocks from the red bed sites show more advanced stages of corrosion and/or oxidation, including dissolution textures (corrosion along fractures and at grain margins, dissolution pits), skeletal trellis textures, and recrystallization. Some did not respond to demagnetization, producing unin- terpretable results. Others have steep and north directed magneti- zations superimposed on a lower intensity, shallow magnetiza- tion component that resembles the ChRM but whose direction is poorly defined (for example Figure 3a; MAD values are greater than about 15ø). Specimens exhibiting this behavior are consid- ered unreliable, and we interpret the steep magnetization as a re- cent (viscous?) overprint. This form of remagnetization may have the effect of biasing Triassic pole estimates toward the J-1 cusp as proposed by Pan and Symons [1993] resulting in in- tegrated, smoothed, rates of APW. But the facts remain that sig- nificant APW occurred during the Late Triassic and that esti- mates of the J-1 cusp on the craton and the plateau agree with one another within the statistical uncertainty. The hypotheses of a \"large\" rotation of the Colorado plateau and a Late Triassic near still-stand of the paleomagnetic pole between-225 and -200 Ma are thus inconsistent with a growing base of pa- leomagnetic data. Conclusions The poles derived from secondary magnetizations in the Te- covas Formation prompt revision of the interpretation of Triassic APW for North America. Despite being secondary magnetiza- tions, whose ages can only be inferred by comparison with extant poles, the west Texas data confirm that the sharpness of the J-1 cusp is not an artifact of any magnitude of Colorado plateau ro- tation and they indicate a fast rate of APW. We have compiled a revised APW path for North America including Colorado plateau data and calculated independent estimates for the rate of apparent polar wander during Triassic time. Barendregt Abstract: Sequences of pre-Wisconsinan till and intercalated paleosols were sampled for paleomagnetic study. The tills were deposited during successive glaciations and the paleosols formed during interglacial intervals. Paleoargillic horizons of the paleosols and the carbonate cement (calcrete) found in some till-paleosol units generally yielded excellent data. Magnetizations of paleosols probably were acquired during the formation of the paleosols rather than during initial deposition of the tills in which they were developed. At Mokowan Butte (Alberta), the lowest paleosol has normal polarity, two of the middle tills have reversed polarity, and the uppermost till - paleosol unit has normal polarity. At Saint Mary Ridge (Montana), three of the lower tills have reversed polarity, and the upper two till-paleosol units have normal polarity. At Two Medicine Ridge (Montana), the lowest three tills are reversed, but the paleoargillic horizon on the uppermost (fourth) till is normal. Magnetostratigraphic correlation indicates that at least six glacial and six interglacial episodes are represented in the Kennedy Drift. The upper normal polarity units are interpreted as having been developed during the Brunhes Normal Chron, the unde

tills in which they were developed. At Mokowan Butte (Alberta), the lowest paleosol has normal polarity, two of the middle tills have reversed polarity, and the uppermost till - paleosol unit has normal polarity. At Saint Mary Ridge (Montana), three of the lower tills have reversed polarity, and the upper two till-paleosol units have normal polarity. At Two Medicine Ridge (Montana), the lowest three tills are reversed, but the paleoargillic horizon on the uppermost (fourth) till is normal. Magnetostratigraphic correlation indicates that at least six glacial and six interglacial episodes are represented in the Kennedy Drift. The upper normal polarity units are interpreted as having been developed during the Brunhes Normal Chron, the underlying reversed polarity sediments during the Matuyama Reversed Chron, and the lowest normal polarity unit at Mokowan Butte during the Gauss Normal Chron. The oldest glaciations here extend into the Pliocene (2600 ka), making these sediments among the oldest glacial deposits in North America. Alternatively, the lowest normally magnetized paleosol at Mokowan Butte may have formed during either the Jaramillo or the Olduvai subchrons, although this is considered less likely. About 500 samples were taken in the southern part of the Ionian Zone in Albania, covering the whole Mesozoic and the Tertiary until Oligocene. By using all available data from Albania (including unpub- lished data by Mauritsch et al.), special attention was paid to the problem of superimposed rota- tions and the significance of the observed direc- tions for the geodynamic evolution of the Ionian Zone. 2. Geological setting and sampling The area under investigation constitutes part of the Ionian Zone, a member of the external zone of the Albanides. In the western part, the Ionian Zone overthrusts the Preapulian foreland, whereas in the eastern part, it is overthrusted by the Kruja Zone and the Cukali-Krasta Zone. Introduction Since the early seventies a number of investi- gators have compiled palaeomagnetic data from the Mediterranean in order to describe and dis- criminate areas with unique rotation senses (Lowrie and Alvarez, 1975; Van den Berg et al., 1978; Channel et al., 1979; Lowrie, 1986; West- phal et al., 1986; Mfirton, 1987; Mauritsch and Becke, 1987). These papers suggest a central realm of counter-clockwise (CCW) rotations rela- tive to the present North, called the Adriatic plate. However, in the Eastern Alps and in the transition zone from the Dinarides into the A1- banides-Hellenides, abrupt changes of this regime have been recognised. Conclusions The palaeomagnetic data presented above sug- gest pre-folding magnetization directions, proved by successful laboratory experiments and field tests. At several sites fold tests were carried out, antipodal directions were found, and results from three different tectonic units were found to be in the same range. The sedimentation of terrigenous flysch deposits was initiated in the Oligocene and continued up to the Lower Miocene. These sediments are over- lain by a Middle and Upper Miocene molasse formation of the pre-Adriatic depression. At the margins of the depression, the Tortonian rests on older formations with angular unconformity. In the southernmost part of Albania, various nappes of the Outer Albanides contain carbona- ceous sediments of Permo-Triassic to Quater- nary age. The nappe and fold structure with an overall north-northwest (NNW) strike allows the application of palaeomagnetic fold tests on a local, as well as on a regional scale. Taking into account all these results, the question arises, whether the Shkoder-Pec Line could be the transition zone between opposing senses of rotation. In the Inner Albanides two phases (Upper Jurassic and Upper Cretaceous) of orogeny are reported, while in the Outer Albanides three phases are evident in Upper Liassic, Lower Miocene and Middle to Upper Miocene (Jacobs- hagen et al., 1978; Pumo et al., 1982). The objective of this study was to complete the information about the geodynamic evolution of Albania presented by Mauritsch et al. (1991), which was based on northern and middle Alba- nian palaeomagnetic data of Mesozoic and Ceno- zoic rocks, sampled in 1989. About 500 samples were taken in the southern part of the Ionian Zone in Albania, covering the whole Mesozoic and the Tertiary until Oligocene. By using all available data from Albania (including unpub- lished data by Mauritsch et al.), special attention was paid to the problem of superimposed rota- tions and the significance of the observed direc- tions for the geodynamic evolution of the Ionian Zone. 2. Geological setting and sampling The area under investigation constitutes part of the Ionian Zone, a member of the external zone of the Albanides. In the western part, the Ionian Zone overthrusts the Preapulian foreland, whereas in the eastern part, it is overthrusted by the Kruja Zone and the Cukali-Krasta Zone. The tectonic features and the lithofacies develop- ment suggest that the Ionian Zone is a remnant of a miogeosynclinal area. Two major tectonic events, in the Lower Miocene and Middle to Upper Miocene, transformed the geosynclinal structure into an intensively folded zone. The sedimentation of terrigenous flysch deposits was initiated in the Oligocene and continued up to the Lower Miocene. These sediments are over- lain by a Middle and Upper Miocene molasse formation of the pre-Adriatic depression. At the margins of the depression, the Tortonian rests on older formations with angular unconformity. In the southernmost part of Albania, various nappes of the Outer Albanides contain carbona- ceous sediments of Permo-Triassic to Quater- nary age. The nappe and fold structure with an overall north-northwest (NNW) strike allows the application of palaeomagnetic fold tests on a local, as well as on a regional scale. The majority of the localities are located along the road from Jorgucat across the Muzine Pass to Delvine (Fig. 2), representing a stratigraphic section from Eocene to Triassic age within a single tectonic unit, the Marl i Gjere structure. Geological setting and sampling The area under investigation constitutes part of the Ionian Zone, a member of the external zone of the Albanides. In the western part, the Ionian Zone overthrusts the Preapulian foreland, whereas in the eastern part, it is overthrusted by the Kruja Zone and the Cukali-Krasta Zone. The tectonic features and the lithofacies develop- ment suggest that the Ionian Zone is a remnant of a miogeosynclinal area. The sedimentation of terrigenous flysch deposits was initiated in the Oligocene and continued up to the Lower Miocene. These sediments are over- lain by a Middle and Upper Miocene molasse formation of the pre-Adriatic depression. At the margins of the depression, the Tortonian rests on older formations with angular unconformity. In the southernmost part of Albania, various nappes of the Outer Albanides contain carbona- ceous sediments of Permo-Triassic to Quater- nary age. The nappe and fold structure with an overall north-northwest (NNW) strike allows the application of palaeomagnetic fold tests on a local, as well as on a regional scale. Seventeen localities were investigated during the sampling campaign in 1991, each comprising up to eleven sites to cover lithologic inhomo- geneities and local structures. The geographic coordinates of the sampling sites and the strati- graphic age are given in Table 1. The majority of the localities are located along the road from Jorgucat across the Muzine Pass to Delvine (Fig. 2), representing a stratigraphic section from Eocene to Triassic age within a single tectonic unit, the Marl i Gjere structure. However, the between-site scatter was very large. Some improvement in the between-site groupings was made by af partial demagnetization in fields of 500 oe. However, even with the improve- ment, the declinations for the site range over more than 180 ø of arc. The inclinations are positive and range between 28 ø and 57 ø, so that no true reversal is present. The large scat- ter between site mean directions is difficult to account for. No pole position has been calc.ulated from these widely dispersed data. DISCUSSION AND i[NTERPRETATION A reliable pole position has been determined for the La Teta lava only. Attempts to improve further the clustering of the La Teta directions of magnetization by making bedding corrections were inconclusive.

The Guajira peninsula is an arid region in northernmost South America, centrally located on the south shores of the Caribbean Sea (Figure 1). Pre-Tertiary rocks here are exposed in isolated topographic and structural highs surrounded by lowlands of fiat-lying Tertiary marine strata. The pre-Tertiary rocks of the peninsula form parallel structural zones of ENE trend [Mac- Donald et al., 1968]. Most site mean directions are close in attitude to the present Earth's Geld and are not indicative of large tectonic rotations. An antipodally reversed direction is obtained at one site by thermal demagnetization, suggesting magnetization in an ancient paleofield nearly coaxial with the present field. Few cratonic Jurassic directions have been re- ported from South America, but at least one such study shows Jurassic paleofield directions close to the present field directions. In defining the Mesozoic polar wander path for South America, distinguishing Jurassic from present field directions will be a continuing challenge. section_candidates.excerpt: OGIC SETTING The Santa Marta massif lies at the northern end of the Colombian Andes. The oldest rocks here are l,300-m.y.-old gneisses which are invaded by numerous batholiths of Jurassic and younger age (MacDonald and Hurley, 1969; Tschanz and others, 1969, 1974). These crystalline rocks are unconformably overlain and partly roofed by Jurassic terrestrial clastic rocks and silicic to basic volcanic rocks. Cretaceous marine strata uncon- formably overlie the Jurassic section. This study presents preliminary paleomagnetic results for Jurassic red beds and volcanic rocks along the southeast flank of the massif (Fig. 1). In the region sampled, the prevailing dip is southeasterly, gentle to moderate. Many Mesozoic formations have been mapped in this area (Tschanz and others, 1969). Fault- ing, facies changes, limited exposure, and scarcity of radiometric age dates complicate the stratigraphic correlation of these strata. The samples include red sedimentary rocks as well as mafic to intermediate or felsic intrusive and extrusive rocks (see Table 1). Standard 2.5-cm cores were drilled from these samples in the laboratory. Paleomagnetic study included measurement of natural re-manent magnetism (NRM) (Schonsted DSM 1) and stepwise alternating field (AF) demagnetization of selected specimens to 70 milliteslas (mT) (700 Oe) using a 2-axis tumbler. Thirty-two specimens were thermally demagnetized in a field <20 nanoteslas (nT) (^20 gamma) to 650 °C. Alteration has affected the plagioclase and oxide grains and caused minor chloritization of the pyroxenes; however, the pyroxene microphenocrysts are usually quite fresh. This probably derives from field observations and isotopic age determinations of Goldsmith and others (1971). They did not date the granite but inferred that it was probably of Early Jurassic age on the basis of its petrographic similarity to three other batholiths to the south which gave near-identical K- Ar (biotite) ages in the range of 192 to 196 ± 7 m.y. They did measure a K-Ar (sanidine) age of 127 ± 3 m.y. on the rhyolite near Ocana. Their location map suggests that the sample locality must have been very close to (if not the same as) our locality II roadcut. ata for basaltic intrusions in the central Falcon Basin document a secondary magnetization associated with alteration during Miocene time. The rocks are extensively altered; however, most of this alteration probably accompanied cooling soon after intrusion. Comparing these secondary magnetic signatures to those of other Ceno- zoic sites in South America, we conclude that magnetization occurred before the late Miocene folding in the basin and soon after intrusion. A later stable partial overprinting of this secondary magnetization occurred in which the present geomagnetic field was superimposed on the stable Miocene rema- nence. At many sites it is difficult to remove this overprinting during demagnetization. The resultant magnetic signature has a steep positive inclination, which in the past has been difficult to interpret. INTRODUCTION The Faltón Basin is an extensional pullapart rift of Neogene age which formed within a complex right-lateral transcurrent fault system along the Venezuelan continental margin. The strati- graphic, structural, and tectonic history of the basin is docu- mented in this volume (Muessig, 1984). The main phase of basin subsidence and filling occurred during Oligocene and Miocene times. Alkaline to subalkaline basaltic sills and dikes intrude

Miocene rema- nence. At many sites it is difficult to remove this overprinting during demagnetization. The resultant magnetic signature has a steep positive inclination, which in the past has been difficult to interpret. INTRODUCTION The Faltón Basin is an extensional pullapart rift of Neogene age which formed within a complex right-lateral transcurrent fault system along the Venezuelan continental margin. The strati- graphic, structural, and tectonic history of the basin is docu- mented in this volume (Muessig, 1984). The main phase of basin subsidence and filling occurred during Oligocene and Miocene times. Alkaline to subalkaline basaltic sills and dikes intrude the Oligocene-Miocene sediments. One of these sills (La Guarabitas, Fig. 1) was dated at 22.9 ± 0.9 m.y. by K-Ar methods (Muessig, 1978). This age is the youngest basaltic activity reported in Venezuela. Only dacites from the Campano area in eastern Venezuela are younger (5 ± 0.5 m.y.; Santamaría and Schubert, 1974). The Faltón Basin was later inverted by compressional events such that the central basin is now the deformed core of the Falcon Anticlinorium. These dikes crosscut sediments and basement rocks associated with the Ponta Grossa Arch, a tectonic feature in the eastern border of the Paleozoic-Mesozoic Paranti Basin. These dikes are vertical or subvertical and trend mainly NW and NE. Samples from 127 dikes were submitted to both alternating field and thermal demagnetizations; 121 of them yielded characteristic directions interpreted as original thermal remanent magnetizations. Both normal and reversed polarities as well as intermediate directions (6 dikes) are recorded. The paleomagnetic pole is located at 30.3øE, 82.4øS (N = 115; c%= 2.0ø; k = 43.8). This pole along with the available paleomagnetic poles for the Paranti Basin volcanics (Serra Geral Formation), recalculated in this paper in the light of reported 40Ar/39Ar ages describe an apparent polar wander path segment corresponding to a clockwise rotation (6.9 ø) of the South American plate. This movement is compatible with the initial phase of th

ration [Almeida, 1986]. Associated with this structure is one of the largest Phanerozoic mafic dike swarms in Brazil: the Poma Grossa dike swarm. Although maps based on aeromagnetic data (Figure 1) show a high concentration of dikes in the central area of the arch (between Rio Alonzo and So Jer6nimo-Curifiva lineaments), dike outcrops are mainly concentrated in the regions of Fartara, Sapopema, and Telmaco Borba, where they intrude the Paleozoic sedimentary rocks of the Paranti Basin, and in the regions of Curitiba and Guapiara, where they intrude the Precambrian rocks of the crystalline basement. Results from integrated ground/airborne magnetometry [ Ussami et al., 1991] demonstrate that the magnetic anomalies currently associated with dikes are actually related to structural features in the crystalline basement. Dike thicknesses vary from tens to hundreds of meters and are often tens of kilometers in length. They are fine to medium grained, and no difference in grain size is evident for dikes cutting Paleozoic or Precambrian terrains. The coarsest-grained diabase was found intruding sediments in the western part of the arch, near Sapopema (Figure 1). This reversal asymmetry is mainly in declination. An artifact of remagnetization cannot be entirely ruled out, but we find this explanation rather unsatisfactory given the lack of systematic magneto-mineralogical or isotope variations (580 and 53C) within these anomalous normal polarity horizons. Dalziel Institute for Geophysics, University of Texas at Austin Abstract. A new - 117 Ma paleomagnetic pole has been defined from the study of volcanic and plutonic rocks from the eastern portion Marie Byrd Land (MBL). The new pole (185.6øE / 56.8øS, A95 = 8.7 ø) implies that the eastern portion of MBL was an integral part of Weddellia, which included the ancestral Antarctic Peninsul

al., 1987a, 1987b, 1991; Grunow, 1993; Dalziel and Grunow, 1992]. However, it has been difficult to form a concise picture of the pre- mid-Cretaceous tectonic evolution due to the remoteness and scattered nature of the rock outcrops and attendant paucity of geological details and the small number of paleomagnetic studies. Most previous plate tectonic reconstructions of West Antarctica have dealt primarily with the crustal blocks of the Weddell Sea sector (AP, TI, and EWM), collectively referred to as \"Weddellia\" by Grunow et al. [1987a], as recent work has progressed westward from the Scotia arc, and hence the largest number of paleomagnetic results are available for these. In paleogeographic reconstructions, MBL is usually left near to its present position close to the Transantarctic Mountains and North Victoria Land because of the similarity of Paleozoic rocks in western MBL and North Victoria Land. The ~100 Ma paleomagnetic results from MBL confirm a position for MBL near North Victoria Land at this time [DiVenere et al., 1994], but there have been no reliable pre-100 Ma paleomagnetic results for MBL. This has created the impression that MBL, and the then-attached New Zealand microcontinent, were not attached to, and have evolved separately from, Weddellia, even 8133 813

No sun compass checks could be made at Mount Matikonis or at Vance/LeMasurier because clouds or outcrop shadows prevented it. Magnetic variation was calculated for each site from the International Geomagnetic Reference Field [Langel, 1992], and appropriate corrections were applied to the field data. Differences between the magnetic and sun compass readings were within 2 ø to 3 ø and the magnetic compass readings were used for the core orientations. All samples .were subjected to either progressive thermal demagnetization to maximum temperatures of 675øC, or progressive alternating field (AF) demagnetization to maximum fields of 100 mT. Both demagnetization methods were used for each site. Specimen directional behavior was similar under both methods, though thermal demagnetization tended to give better results for the granodiorites while AF demagnetization gave good results in the volcanic rocks. Measurements were made on an ScT two-axis cryogenic magnetometer, or a Digico spinner magnetometer for very strongly magnetized samples. Bulk magnetic susceptibility was monitored using a Barrington susceptibility bridge for all specimens after each therm

le space. Magnetic component directions were calculated by principal component analysis [Kirschvink, 1980] of linear segments chosen by inspection from orthogonal plots [Zijderveld, 1967]. The components thus determined were plotted on equal-area nets, and mean directions were determined by standard Fisher statistics [Fisher, 1953]. However, it has been difficult to form a concise picture of the pre- mid-Cretaceous tectonic evolution due to the remoteness and scattered nature of the rock outcrops and attendant paucity of geological details and the small number of paleomagnetic studies. Most previous plate tectonic reconstructions of West Antarctica have dealt primarily with the crustal blocks of the Weddell Sea sector (AP, TI, and EWM), collectively referred to as \"Weddellia\" by Grunow et al. However, it has been difficult to form a concise picture of the pre- mid-Cretaceous tectonic evolution due to the remoteness and scattered nature of the rock outcrops and attendant paucity of geological details and the small number of paleomagnetic studies. Most previous plate tectonic reconstructions of West Antarctica have dealt primarily with the crustal blocks of the Weddell Sea sector (AP, TI, and EWM), collectively referred to as \"Weddellia\" by Grunow et al. [1987a], as recent work has progressed westward from the Scotia arc, and hence the largest number of paleomagnetic results are available for these. In paleogeographic reconstructions, MBL is usually left near to its present position close to the Transantarctic Mountains and North Victoria Land because of the similarity of Paleozoic rocks in western MBL and North Victoria Land. Geological Background The geologic record of western MBL begins with a lower Paleozoic turbidire sequence, the Swanson Formation, which was folded and mildly metamorphosed in Late Ordovician time [Adams, 1986]. Similar rocks are found on Campbell Island of the southern Campbell Plateau as well as constituting the Greenland Group of western South Island, New Zealand [Adams, 1986]. The Robertson Bay Group of North Victoria Land, on the edge of the East Antarctic craton, is sedimentalogically similar to the Swanson Formation and Greenland Group [Bradshaw et al., 1983] and has often been correlated with them, although metamorphism in the rocks of MBL and New Zealand appears to postdate the Cambro- Ordovician Ross Orogeny in North Victoria Land by about 50 Ma [Adams, 1986]. However, we judge the Mount Vance/LeMasurier volcanics results to be the most reliable estimate of the Early Cretaceous pole position. They are supported by a positive contact test with the intruding -100 Ma syenite, as described above, implying that the magnetization in the volcanics predates the 100 Ma intrusion. The volcanic bedding was used to tilt-correct the 100 Ma syenites which provided a positive regional tilt-test for the -100 Ma intrusions on the Ruppert/Hobbs Coast [DiVenere et al., 1994], supporting the assumption that the bedding gives a good approximation of the paleohorizontal. Dalziel Institute for Geophysics, University of Texas at Austin Abstract. A new - 117 Ma paleomagnetic pole has been defined from the study of volcanic and plutonic rocks from the eastern portion Marie Byrd Land (MBL). The new pole (185.6øE / 56.8øS, A95 = 8.7 ø) implies that the eastern portion of MBL was an integral part of Weddellia, which included the ancestral Antarctic Peninsul

al., 1987a, 1987b, 1991; Grunow, 1993; Dalziel and Grunow, 1992]. However, it has been difficult to form a concise picture of the pre- mid-Cretaceous tectonic evolution due to the remoteness and scattered nature of the rock outcrops and attendant paucity of geological details and the small number of paleomagnetic studies. Most previous plate tectonic reconstructions of West Antarctica have dealt primarily with the crustal blocks of the Weddell Sea sector (AP, TI, and EWM), collectively referred to as \"Weddellia\" by Grunow et al. [1987a], as recent work has progressed westward from the Scotia arc, and hence the largest number of paleomagnetic results are available for these. New Miocene Paleomagnetic and Geochronologic Results Until recently, the Andean basins of Bolivia have been relatively poorly studied in contrast to, for example, the classic Cenozoic exposures of Argentina. Starting in the 1960s, fossil mammals were recovered from several sites in the Altiplano and Cordillera of Bolivia [Hoffstetter, 1968; Hoffstetter et al., 1972; Villarroel, 1974]. At about the same time, volcanic samples were collected that provided initial calibrations for some of these basin sequences [e.g., Evernden et al., 1977]. With the advent of magnetic polarity stratigraphy and the presence of long, relatively continuous and highly fossiliferous sections, the chronology of middle and late Cenozoic Andean basins of Bolivia advanced significantly. MacFadden et al. [1985] and Naeser et al. [1987] presented the chronology of Salla, one of the older, i.e., late Oligocene/early Miocene basin deposits. Swisher III Berkeley Geochronology Laboratory, Berkeley, California Abstract. Geophysical and tectonic evidence suggests that the principal vertical axis bending of the Bolivian Orocline is a late Cenozoic event related to subduction and Andean uplift. To further test this hypothesis, paleomagnetic data are presented from Miocene basins within the Altiplano and Cordillera Oriental of Bolivia, located in the presumed southern limb of the orocline. To factor out potential VGP data, samples were collected from sedimentary sections spanning at least 0.5 m.y. New paleomagnetic data are presented for two sites, i.e., Cerdas (21øS latitude, 16-15 Ma) and Quehua (20øS latitude, 13-7 Ma). In conjunction with previously published paleomagnetic results from middle to late Tertiary rocks from Bolivia and Peru spanning some 16 ø of latitude (6-22øS), a consistent pattern of oroclinal development is as follows: significant counterclockwise rotation (about 15-20 ø ) in the northern limb, negligible rotation in the axis (at the latitude of the Arica Deflection), and significant clockwise rotation (about 15-20 ø) in the southern limb

ificant clockwise rotation (about 15-20 ø) in the southern limb. Although these paleomagnetic data could represent independent, mesoscale (>102 to <104 km 2) block rotations, the preferred interpretation is that they confirm the hypothesis that a significant portion (about 30-40 ø) of the oroclinal bending occurred during the late Cenozoic. Using the unit mean paleomagnetic declinations in the well- dated sections, minimum rates of oroclinal bending during the late Cenozoic are calculated to range from 0.6ø/m.y. to 1.7ø/m.y. The remaining 15-20 ø of observed curvature of the orocline probably resulted from an earlier phase of Andean deformation or may represent the shape of the ancestral Andes. Introduction In plan view many of the orogenic zones of the world are distinctly arcuate, and classically, it has been assumed that this reflects the original continent-wide shape of the mountain range. In contrast, Carey [1955] proposed the concept of an orocline to describe large-scale, vertical axis bending of mountain ranges that have occurred during orogenesis. Carey [1958] also coined the term \"Bolivian Orocline\" to describe the approximately 45' bend observed in the central Andes at the so-called \"Arica Deflection,\" which is the presumed oroclinal axis. The prediction is that paleomagnetic vectors, or so-called \"declination anomalies,\" from late Tertiary sediments lying in the southern limb of the orocline will show a pattern of uniform, clockwise, vertical axis rotations, whereas those from the northern limb will show counterclockwise rotations, both resulting from deformation during the later phase of Andean orogeny. There are essentially two schools of thought that exist with regard to the origin of the shape of the Andes, i.e., oroclinal bending versus mesoscale in situ block rotation. The field and laboratory procedures were similar for the two new localities discussed below, i.e., Cerdas and Quehua. Accordingly, the paleomagnetic field and laboratory methods and results for both localities are discussed here. The interpretation of the magnetostratigraphy and correlation to the magnetic polarity time scale (MPTS) are resented separately below after the discussion of the Ar/39Ar age determinations. Swisher III Berkeley Geochronology Laboratory, Berkeley, California Abstract. Geophysical and tectonic evidence suggests that the principal vertical axis bending of the Bolivian Orocline is a late Cenozoic event related to subduction and Andean uplift. To further test this hypothesis, paleomagnetic data are presented from Miocene basins within the Altiplano and Cordillera Oriental of Bolivia, located in the presumed southern limb of the orocline. To factor out potential VGP data, samples were collected from sedimentary sections spanning at least 0.5 m.y. New paleomagnetic data are presented for two sites, i.e., Cerdas (21øS latitude, 16-15 Ma) and Quehua (20øS latitude, 13-7 Ma). In conjunction with previously published paleomagnetic results from middle to late Tertiary rocks from Bolivia and Peru spanning some 16 ø of latitude (6-22øS), a consistent pattern of oroclinal development is as follows: significant counterclockwise rotation (about 15-20 ø ) in the northern limb, negligible rotation in the axis (at the latitude of the Arica Deflection), and significant clockwise rotation (about 15-20 ø) in the southern limb

ificant clockwise rotation (about 15-20 ø) in the southern limb. Although these paleomagnetic data could represent independent, mesoscale (>102 to <104 km 2) block rotations, the preferred interpretation is that they confirm the hypothesis that a significant portion (about 30-40 ø) of the oroclinal bending occurred during the late Cenozoic. Using the unit mean paleomagnetic declinations in the well- dated sections, minimum rates of oroclinal bending during the late Cenozoic are calculated to range from 0.6ø/m.y. to 1.7ø/m.y. The remaining 15-20 ø of observed curvature of the orocline probably resulted from an earlier phase of Andean deformation or may represent the shape of the ancestral Andes. Introduction In plan view many of the orogenic zones of the world are distinctly arcuate, and classically, it has been assumed that this reflects the original continent-wide shape of the mountain range. In contrast, Carey [1955] proposed the concept of an orocline to describe large-scale, vertical axis bending of mountain ranges that have occurred during orogenesis. Carey [1958] also coined the term \"Bolivian Orocline\" to describe the approximately 45' bend observed in the central Andes at the so-called \"Arica Deflection,\" which is the presumed oroclinal axis. Since Carey's i

The prediction is that paleomagnetic vectors, or so-called \"declination anomalies,\" from late Tertiary sediments lying in the southern limb of the orocline will show a pattern of uniform, clockwise, vertical axis rotations, whereas those from the northern limb will show counterclockwise rotations, both resulting from deformation during the later phase of Andean orogeny. Bolivian Orocline and Andean Tectonics There is a diversity of opinion about the origin of the arcuate shape of the Andes and whether or not it fits the notion of oroclinal bending first proposed by Carey [ 1955, 1958] and later refined in light of plate tectonic theory [e.g., lsacks, 1988]. There are essentially two schools of thought that exist with regard to the origin of the shape of the Andes, i.e., oroclinal bending versus mesoscale in situ block rotation. A related question is the timing of the Andean orogeny, as is also discussed below. Oroclinal Bending As mentioned above, Carey
